objectives: State the game loop's frame structure.

slides.title: The game loop
slides.body:
Every game runs the same skeleton:
```
while (running) {
  input = poll_input();
  update_state(input, dt);
  render(state);
  sleep_until_next_frame();
}
```

At 60 frames per second (FPS) = 16.67 ms per frame. The CPU + GPU must finish all work in that window. At 30 FPS = 33 ms. At VR-friendly 90 FPS = 11 ms. At 120 FPS = 8.33 ms.

**Frame breakdown** (typical):
- Input poll: ~0.1 ms.
- Game-state update: 1-5 ms (game logic, AI, physics).
- Render setup (CPU): 1-3 ms (culling, draw call submission).
- GPU render: 5-12 ms.
- VSync wait: rest.

**Frame timing modes**:
- **VSync ON**: frame buffer flips on monitor refresh; locks to 60/120/144 Hz. Eliminates tearing but caps frame rate.
- **VSync OFF**: render as fast as possible. Visible tearing on screen.
- **FreeSync / G-Sync**: monitor refreshes when GPU is ready. Best of both.

**The frame-time budget is the central engineering constraint of a game**. Late frames cause stutter, perceptible as jitter or input lag. Indie devs target 60 FPS at 1080p; AAA devs target 60 FPS at 4K. VR demands ≥90 FPS with low motion-to-photon latency (<20 ms) to avoid nausea.

**Profile-driven optimization**: tools like RenderDoc, NVIDIA Nsight, Intel GPA, Unity Profiler, Unreal Insights show where time goes per frame. The 80/20 rule applies: a few systems dominate cost; optimize those.

slides.title: Fixed vs variable timestep
Entity-Component-System (ECS) architecture
slides.body:
Traditional OOP game architecture: deep inheritance hierarchies (`Entity → MovingEntity → AICharacter → Enemy → Boss`). Brittle, hard to extend, poor cache locality.

**Entity-Component-System** (Bilas 2002+, Unity DOTS 2018+):
- **Entity**: an ID. Just a number.
- **Component**: pure data, no behavior. `Position`, `Velocity`, `Health`, `Sprite`.
- **System**: pure logic operating on components. `PhysicsSystem` queries entities with `Position + Velocity` + advances them.

An entity 'has' a set of components. Composition over inheritance: a Player is `Position + Velocity + Health + Sprite + PlayerInput`. An Enemy is `Position + Velocity + Health + Sprite + AI`. Adding a new behavior = adding a component + a system that uses it.

**Data-Oriented Design (DOD)**: store components in tight arrays (one array per component type). `PhysicsSystem` iterates Position-array + Velocity-array contiguously → cache-friendly → 10-100× faster than scattered pointer chasing.

```cpp
// ECS pseudo-code (Unity DOTS-style)
for (int i = 0; i < positions.length; i++) {
  positions[i] += velocities[i] * dt;
}
// CPU prefetches both arrays; SIMD-friendly; vectorizes.
```

Compare to OOP:
```cpp
for (auto& obj : entities) {
  obj.position += obj.velocity * dt;  // pointer indirection per entity, cache misses
}
```

**Major ECS implementations**:
- **Unity DOTS** (Burst + ECS + Jobs): high-performance multithreaded game systems.
- **Bevy** (Rust): pure-ECS engine, increasingly popular.
- **EnTT** (C++): popular header-only library.
- **flecs**: another C++ ECS.

**When ECS overshoots**: simple games / GUI / non-perf-critical → OOP is fine. ECS shines when you have many similar entities (particles, units in RTS, bullet hell). Modern engines support both — use ECS for performance-critical components, classes for high-level game flow.

question.question: Compute frame-time budget allocation
question.goal: Target 60 FPS = 16.67 ms / frame. Game with: input (1 ms), physics (4 ms), AI (3 ms), animation (2 ms), CPU render submission (2 ms), GPU draw (?), VSync wait (?).

steps.prompt: If GPU takes 5 ms, the frame misses 60 FPS. Solutions?

options: Move CPU work off the critical path: multithread (Job system); reduce AI tick rate (e.g., 30 Hz instead of 60); reduce physics frequency or precision; reduce draw calls via batching.

steps.reveal: Multithread CPU work (jobs running in parallel); reduce non-essential tick rates (AI 30 Hz, fine for most game AI); GPU optimization (LOD, occlusion culling, fewer draw calls). 60 FPS budget is unforgiving — modern engines push CPU to multiple cores aggressively.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{60 FPS = 16.67 ms — every system fights for a slice}}$$ The frame budget drives every architectural decision. Multi-threaded job systems (Unity's C# Jobs + Burst, Unreal's Task Graph, Doom Eternal's job system) let CPU work overlap. GPU pipelining (3+ frames in flight) decouples GPU from CPU. Frame pacing tooling (e.g., RenderDoc Frame Capture, NVIDIA Reflex) optimizes end-to-end latency for competitive games.

question.question: A new gameplay programmer uses variable timestep + finds the physics behaves differently when the player is on a 30 FPS laptop vs 144 FPS gaming PC. Bug?
options: Yes — variable timestep physics is frame-rate-dependent. Switch to FIXED-timestep physics (e.g., 60 Hz) + interpolated rendering for stable cross-platform behavior.
question.explanation: Variable timestep makes physics integration unstable + non-deterministic. Different framerates produce different game states. Fix: fixed physics timestep (decouple from render rate); interpolate visual representation between fixed updates for smooth rendering. Standard practice (Gaffer 'Fix Your Timestep!'). Every major engine + every competitive multiplayer game does this.

slides.workedSolution: Variable timestep means physics integration step size differs by framerate. Numerical integrators (Euler, Verlet, RK4) have step-size-dependent error. At 30 FPS + 144 FPS, same scene diverges. Fix: fixed-timestep physics + interpolate render. Engine setting in Unity, Unreal, Godot. Critical for replays + multiplayer determinism.

Migrating to ECS
question.prompt: Your game has 10,000 enemies + frame time spikes when many are on screen. Walk through whether ECS architecture would help + the migration approach.
Explain in two or three sentences why the game loop's fixed-timestep + variable-render pattern dominates modern game engines.
question.rubric: Mentions that fixed timestep makes physics + AI deterministic + frame-rate-independent (essential for replays + multiplayer); variable rendering with interpolation keeps the visual smooth at any framerate; the pattern decouples simulation from presentation. Every major engine (Unity, Unreal, Godot) defaults to this; deviating from it leads to physics bugs + multiplayer desyncs.
